strengths: Introduces a novel, well-motivated gradient-free bi-objective (stretch-and-squeeze) framework that unifies invariance discovery and adversarial attack generation under a common formalism, addressing a real gap between MEI-based feature visualization and invariance characterization.

Comprehensive experimental validation: pixel-space distance analyses, SVC discriminability of invariant image classes across layers, representational distance analysis across the network hierarchy, and human/observer-network psychophysics, all converging on a coherent hierarchical story (luminance/contrast at low levels, texture at mid levels, pose/viewpoint at high levels).

Interesting and non-trivial comparative finding between robust and standard networks (robust network invariant images are more human/CNN recognizable, with opposing depth-dependent trends), which connects to and extends prior metamer literature (Feather et al.) in a meaningful way.

Reasonably strong human-subject psychophysics methodology (pre-registered-style screening, GLMM with FDR correction, comparison to multiple observer CNNs) and thoughtful robustness checks (subsampling of representational space) relevant to potential neuroscience applications.

Method is model-agnostic and demonstrated to work with hidden-layer targets and heavily subsampled representations, suggesting practical applicability to real neurophysiology experiments with limited recording capacity.
Code and data availability stated (open-source), aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Evaluation is restricted to a single subject architecture (ResNet-50, standard vs. one L2-robust variant); no experiments on other architectures (e.g., ViTs, other CNN families) despite the paper's claims of general applicability, weakening claims about generality of the hierarchical invariance findings.

The optimization convergence statistics (Supplementary A.3) show that many invariance searches at mid/high levels did not converge (e.g., only 5.84%-32.60% converged for standard network high_level/mid_level), raising concerns about how much of the reported qualitative/quantitative trends are influenced by non-converged runs, though the authors argue final populations still reach functionally relevant activation regimes.

The generative prior (a fixed pretrained deep generator, fc7-based) inherently constrains and biases the space of "invariant" images that can be discovered, which is somewhat in tension with the claim of an "unbiased" framework; this limitation is not deeply discussed.

No direct in vivo/biological neural data is used; all "neuroscience applicability" claims rest on simulated subsampling of artificial network units, so the paper's translational claims to biological visual systems remain speculative until validated experimentally (acknowledged as future work, but this tempers the significance claims in the abstract/discussion).

Quantitative effect sizes for some key claims (e.g., correlation of human vs. observer-network accuracy patterns in Fig. 5d) are described qualitatively ("highly correlated") without always reporting explicit correlation coefficients or statistical tests in the main text.
The paper's discussion of why larger/higher-performing standard networks show different recognizability trends is somewhat speculative and not further tested with additional experiments or controls.

Only one robust-training configuration (L2, eps=3) is tested; robustness findings might not generalize across different robust training recipes (L_inf, different epsilon values, different architectures) since the choice of ε or norm type could significantly change invariance geometry.

strengths: The paper proposes a well-motivated bi-objective (stretch/squeeze) gradient-free framework that unifies invariance discovery and adversarial-example generation under a single formalism, which is a reasonably elegant reframing of two previously separate lines of work.

The empirical evaluation is fairly comprehensive: SVC-based separability analysis, representational distance analysis across layers, a carefully designed human psychophysics experiment (25 participants, proper screening, GLMM statistics with FDR correction), and replication with multiple observer CNNs (standard and robust).

The comparison between standard and adversarially robust ResNet50 yields an interesting and consistent pattern (robust invariances more human/CNN recognizable, opposite depth-trends between robust and standard models), which is consistent with and extends prior metamer literature.
The robustness-to-subsampling experiments are a nice applied contribution suggesting potential utility for neuroscience settings where only sparse neural populations can be recorded.
Reasonable transparency on methodology (pseudocode, hyperparameters, compute resources, and a stated intent to release code), aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The empirical validation is restricted essentially to a single architecture family (ResNet50, standard vs. one L2-robust variant); despite claims of being 'model-agnostic,' no other architectures (e.g., ViTs, other CNN families) or datasets are tested, so generality is unverified and explicitly left to future work.

The claim of being an 'unbiased' method is questionable since the search is still restricted to the manifold spanned by a specific (and relatively old, low-fidelity) image generator (Dosovitskiy & Brox fc7-GAN), which itself imposes a strong natural-image prior that could shape which invariances are discoverable.

Novelty is somewhat overstated: closely related work already explores gradient-free feature landscapes around MEs (e.g., Wang & Ponce 2022, cited as ref [31]) and gradientless metamer-style invariance search (XDREAM); the paper's core empirical finding (robust networks yield more human-interpretable invariances) largely reconfirms Feather et al. 2023 rather than establishing a qualitatively new scientific result.

Despite substantial emphasis on neuroscience applicability, there is no actual biological validation — the 'neuroscience relevance' experiments are entirely simulated by subsampling artificial CNN units, not real neural recordings, so the central translational claim remains speculative.
The AlexNet observer analysis uses only a single response per image (no repeats), which the authors themselves note limits reliability of that comparison.

No ablations or sensitivity analyses regarding key design choices (generator choice, CMA-ES population size/step size, number of Pareto-front iterations) are provided to demonstrate robustness of the method's conclusions to these choices.
The number of target units evaluated (77 readout units) is relatively small and their representativeness within the full 1000-class ImageNet space is not discussed.
Figures are dense with many small sub-panels and use inconsistent color/axis conventions across figures, which hampers readability and makes some quantitative claims hard to verify visually.

No comparison to simpler, non-evolutionary gradient-free baselines is provided to isolate exactly how much of SnS's advantage stems from the bi-objective Pareto formulation versus the underlying generator/optimizer.

strengths: Novel unifying framework (Stretch-and-Squeeze) that casts invariance discovery and adversarial attack generation as a single bi-objective, gradient-free optimization problem, moving beyond feature visualization limited to most-exciting images or predefined transformations (e.g., affine).

Model-agnostic and gradient-free design makes the method broadly applicable, including to settings without a differentiable model, which is directly relevant to neuroscience applications where only black-box or sparsely-sampled neural recordings are available.

Thorough and multi-pronged validation: quantitative representational distance analyses, SVC-based separability of invariant images by processing stage, and a well-powered human psychophysics experiment (with GLMM statistics and multiple-comparison correction) complemented by multiple observer CNNs (standard and robust, varying capacity).

Interesting and consistent qualitative/quantitative findings: hierarchical invariances (luminance/contrast → texture → pose) and clear perceptual differences between standard and adversarially robust networks, replicated across humans and several observer networks, adding to the literature on robust networks as better perceptual models.

Useful robustness check showing that the method's conclusions are largely preserved under heavy subsampling of the representation space (as few as 100 units), directly supporting feasibility for real electrophysiology/imaging experiments with limited neuron counts.
Reasonably detailed methodological transparency (pseudocode, hyperparameters, early-stopping criteria, compute resources) and stated intent to release code.
weaknesses: All core experiments are conducted on a single architecture family (ResNet-50, standard vs. one adversarially robust variant); generality of the hierarchical invariance findings to other architectures (e.g., transformers, other CNNs) is not empirically tested, despite being flagged as future work.

The image generator (a pretrained GAN-like network) imposes a strong natural-image prior; the discovered 'invariance manifold' is therefore bounded by what the generator can produce, so the method characterizes invariance within the generator's learned image statistics rather than the unit's true invariance in unconstrained pixel space. This limitation is only briefly acknowledged.

Optimization convergence is uneven and sometimes quite low (e.g., only ~5.8% convergence for high-level targets in the standard network, and appreciable non-convergence rates elsewhere), raising questions about how representative the reported invariant images are of the full population of optimization runs and whether cherry-picking of converged results could bias qualitative claims.

No real biological neural recordings are used; the neuroscience-applicability claims rest solely on subsampling simulations of ResNet-50 units in silico, rather than any in vivo validation, which the authors themselves note as an open next step.

Baseline comparisons are somewhat narrow — the paper contrasts against predefined affine transformations and XDREAM-style MEIs, but does not compare against other plausible gradient-free or hybrid approaches to invariance discovery, limiting the ability to judge SnS's relative advantage in efficiency or fidelity.

Statistical/quantitative claims (e.g., percentage activation reduction, pixel distances) are reported as means without always contextualizing effect sizes relative to appropriate null distributions beyond the specific controls chosen, and some figures (e.g., Fig. 5c/d) are dense and could benefit from clearer explanation in the main text.

The human psychophysics study, while well-executed, uses relatively few images per condition per participant (5 per category) and a restricted image set (12 categories), which may limit statistical power and generalizability of the recognizability conclusions.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel, well-motivated gradient-free framework (SnS) that unifies invariance and adversarial-vulnerability probing within a single bi-objective (Pareto) optimization, addressing a real gap left by gradient-based metamer/MEI approaches that require differentiable models.

Extensive and carefully designed experimental validation: quantitative pixel-distance and representational-distance analyses, PCA/SVC layer-discriminability tests, intrinsic dimensionality estimation (PCA and 2NN-ID), convergence diagnostics, and single-loss ablations that convincingly demonstrate the necessity of the dual stretch/squeeze objective.

Strong generalizability demonstration across architectures (ResNet50/18, VGG16, Wide-ResNet, DenseNet, ShuffleNet, ViT, CLIP-ViT) and robustness regimes (L2 and L∞ adversarial training), plus robustness to representation subsampling, directly supporting the claimed applicability to neuroscience settings with sparse recordings.

Human psychophysics experiment (n=25, well-powered 12-AFC task with proper GLMM/Wald chi-square statistics and multiple-comparison correction) combined with multiple observer CNNs yields a novel and interesting empirical finding: L2-robust networks lose interpretability advantage at deep layers, diverging from the standard narrative that robustification uniformly improves human alignment.

Thorough, well-organized supplementary material (34 pages) that substantially strengthens the paper's scientific rigor, including comparisons to metamers, computational resource/reproducibility details, and pseudocode.
weaknesses: The method's expressivity and 'unbiased' invariance discovery are fundamentally bounded by the chosen fc7-based image generator (Dosovitskiy & Brox), which imposes its own prior on the image manifold; this caveat is acknowledged only briefly in the limitations and could substantially shape the reported qualitative/quantitative trends (e.g., lack of high-frequency textures, smoothness of invariant images).

The central neuroscience motivation (applicability to biological recordings) is validated only through subsampling simulations on CNN units, not through any actual biological or in vivo data, so claims of neuroscience readiness remain speculative.

Some interpretive claims (e.g., that SnS 'discovers the actual image variation axes' rather than axes constrained by the generator, or characterizations of qualitative invariance types as luminance/texture/pose) rely on informal visual/qualitative description and could benefit from more rigorous, generator-independent verification.

The comparison between robust and standard network interpretability trends, while striking, is demonstrated primarily on a single generator and largely on ResNet50 variants for the main narrative (with only partial ViT/L∞ extensions in the appendix); the core mechanistic explanation for why L2 robustness fails to help in deep layers is not deeply investigated beyond the empirical observation.

Reproducibility text mentions code and data availability links that appear redacted/incomplete in the provided version, and hyperparameter sensitivity (e.g., CMA-ES population size, generator choice, early-stopping thresholds) is not extensively explored.
